articles.text: Following a clear mandate from the school board and strong support from Superintendent Jennifer Hawn, Piedmont Unified School District is preparing for one of its most ambitious program expansions in recent years. Funds have been allocated to add new offerings in world languages, performing arts, and advanced academic coursework—changes aimed at better preparing students for an increasingly competitive college admissions landscape. But as the district looks to move swiftly on these enhancements, teachers—the ones tasked with turning plans into reality— are urging a more deliberate approach to ensure quality and sustainability. With summer less than two months away, the 2025- 2026 master schedule remains in flux. For high school students, new offerings include the rigorous AP Capstone pathway, AP Physics C, a restored Vocal Music program, and dual enrollment through Berkeley City College for Calculus III. At the middle school level, 7th graders will now have access to Level 1 classes in Spanish, French, and Mandarin. This marks a return to a more robust foreign language offering after a recent shift removed language classes to accommodate a new Health course. At the elementary level, the district is exploring the possibility of expanding performing arts and introducing world language instruction, 100 minutes per week, for 4th and 5th graders. The proposal has raised logistical concerns from educators, who are supportive of enriching the curriculum but mindful of existing time constraints. “Teachers are supportive of these changes, but also recognize the complexity of making room for all these programs without losing the best of what we offer students now. articles.text: The City of Piedmont celebrated the 100th anniversary of the dedication of Piedmont Community Hall and the Exedra on Friday, April 4, at Community Hall. The evening transformed the historic hall into a pop-up history exhibit, featuring photos, newspaper clippings, and archival video that took residents on a journey through the city’s past. The event also included live period music, birthday cake, and refreshments. Community Hall and the Exedra were originally dedicated on April 3, 1925, as part of architect Albert Farr’s 1922 Civic Center master plan. The plan envisioned a library, museum, municipal market square, underground streetcar tunnel, and a new City Hall on Guilford Place—but only the Community Hall and Exedra were ultimately built. Piedmont resident and historian Cameron Wolfe offered historical context to attendees about the significance of the Exedra and Community Hall. “The Greeks referred to an ‘Exedra’ as a structure that would provide a place for people to gather behind it and have conversation and fellowship together,” A Piedmont resident reads about the history of Piedmont’s public architecture.

articles.text: The Salvation Army’s 10th Annual Gala, The Way Out 2025 – A Night for Others, reached unprecedented heights this year, raising a remarkable $532,000— breaking all previous records and providing vital resources for those in need across Alameda County. Held at the elegant Claremont Country Club, the sold-out event was a stirring celebration of generosity, community, and the transformative power of the Salvation Army’s life-saving programs. A centerpiece of the evening was the presentation of the Volunteer of the Year Award to Alice Waters, the legendary chef, restaurateur, and champion of sustainable food practices. Waters, best known as the founder of Chez Panisse in Berkeley and a pioneer of the farm-to-table movement, has spent her career advocating for healthy food systems and educational initiatives like the Edible Schoolyard Project, which empowers children to learn about food production and nutrition. In her deeply personal acceptance speech, Waters shared a moving story of her childhood, recounting how, growing up with three sisters, her family could never afford new clothes. It was the Salvation Army thrift store that provided them with everything they needed—a testament to the profound and lasting impact the organization has had on her life. Lt. Col. Bettie Love (LEFT), Alice Waters, Kate Addiego, and Gala co-chair Debbie Kelley. The evening was further electrified by a thrilling auction, which included an exclusive dinner at Chez Panisse with Waters. In a heartwarming display of generosity, she not only extended the offer to include two more guests but also allowed the auctioneer to sell it twice—raising an incredible $25,000 in the process. This stunning gesture was just one of many ways the event brought the community together in support of the Salvation Army’s mission to break the cycle of poverty, homelessness, and hunger. A particularly emotional moment came when Jeff Taylor, a beneficiary of the Salvation Army’s programs, took the stage Lt. Col. Bettie Love (left) at the podium with Alice Waters. to share his powerful personal testimony. His story of overcoming adversity through the organization’s support moved the audience to tears and served as a poignant reminder of the essential role these services play in transforming lives. “This record-breaking event is a testament to the power of community,” said Debbie Kelley, chair of the gala committee and a member of the advisory board. “When we come together and give just a little, we can achieve so much. Tonight, we’ve shown that we can truly make a difference in the lives of individuals and families in need through compassion and generosity.” The funds raised will support the Salvation Army’s crucial programs across Alameda County. These programs provide shelter, food, education, and vocational training to those in need. With five properties across the county—including the only family shelter in the area that accepts boys over the age of 12—the Salvation Army continues to be a beacon of hope for thousands. For more information on The Salvation Army’s ongoing work or to contribute, visit www.alamedawayout.org. A handful of auction items are still available for sale, including a week at Cal’s Lair of the Bear Family camp. The auction page can be found at https://sadeloro2025.ggo.bid/bidding/package-browse. articles.text: Doesn’t it seem like you just paid your property taxes recently? If so, that’s because you did. The prior installment was due on December 10, 2024, and here it is – only four months later – that the Tax Collector is knocking at your door. Owners of real property in California pay property taxes twice a year, with the second installment due on April 10th. Missing the deadline is a very expensive mistake, since you will incur a penalty of 10% plus a $10 fee. If you don’t pay by June 30th, things start to get worse very quickly. Trust me on that. You can send a check, along with your 2nd payment voucher, or pay by phone. However, most people find it more convenient to pay online. The Alameda County Tax Collector’s secure URL for making payments is: https://www.acgov.org/propertytax/index.htm If you want to use a credit card and get those frequent flyer miles, you can do so, but you pay a 2.5% processing fee (the money does not go to the county). A direct debit to your bank account does not incur any additional charges. Although there are several electronic payment services (PayPal and Venmo, to name a few) in common use these days, the Tax Collector has a specific warning about PayPal on its website: NOTICE TO TAXPAYERS USING PAYPAL At this time, we are strongly discouraging the use of PayPal for your property tax payments. Using this method of payment may result in late fees and costs. With our current technology, we can only accept full payments for property taxes; partial payments are not allowed. articles.text: Piedmont City Council held a first reading at their Council meeting on Monday, April 17 for an ordinance that would permanently close the Linda Beach OffLeash Dog Area. The Ordinance would go into effect 30 days after a second reading on April 21. The topic was brought forward quickly when City Staff was contacted by the San Francisco Regional Water Quality Control Board on February 6, regarding a citizen complaint about Linda Park’s Off-Leash Dog Area. The complaint, raising concerns about soil and animal excrement washing down the City’s storm drains, could cost the City as much as $66,000 per day in fines if it does not take action to address the Water Board’s request. Staff recommended that City Council approve the closure of Linda Park’s off-leash area, and the Council voted unanimously to move forward with the closure of the off-leash area. Concurrently, the City will begin a study with the intention to look at how the City can be a good steward of Piedmont’s parks, with an eye toward all uses that serve the needs of the community – including off-leash dog uses. “Staff takes tremendous pride in maintaining our public spaces. That’s something that we’re very proud of,” said Public Works Director Daniel Gonzales. “We maintain these spaces not just in the fashion that it keeps them open to the public but keeps them vibrant and well managed… when we fail to achieve that in one of our spaces, it’s not just frustrating to the public – it’s tremendously frustrating to staff, because our goal is to keep spaces open and keep them working well.” The Off-Leash Area was designated by City ordinance in December 2000, and is often closed during periods of heavy rainfall when the soil becomes muddy and unstable. According to City Staff the area’s sloped hillsides may never have been a good fit for dogs. “Over time we have seen clear evidence of soil erosion. There’s been deterioration of the ivy ground cover, exposing soil and tree roots, and it’s been very evident that active dog play and off-leash dog use has prevented vegetation from regrowing at the area as well,” said Sustainability Program Manager Denise Ergun. The topic will return to City Council for a second reading at their Monday, April 21 meeting later this month. Public Works Director Daniel Gonzales addresses the City Council.

articles.text: Over the past few years, we’ve lost something precious—something many of us didn’t even realize we were missing until it was gone. Community. Not the kind you “follow” or “like” online, but the kind where someone borrows a cup of sugar, where kids ride bikes together down the block, where spontaneous laughter rings out over a shared meal. COVID accelerated this disconnection, but even before the pandemic, our shared spaces were already eroding. Busy schedules, digital distractions, and modern life have chipped away at our instinct to gather. But here’s the thing: rebuilding community doesn’t require a huge event or perfectly planned retreat. It just takes intentionality—and a bit of creativity. Creative Simplicity Is the Key We don’t need to add more to our plates—we need to reframe what’s already there. Here are a few easy, creative ways to cultivate real connection: • The Block Party Potluck: Don’t overthink it. Pick a day, put flyers in a few mailboxes or group texts, and ask people to bring a dish. Add chalk for the kids and a Bluetooth speaker for ambiance. Community will take care of the rest. • Cross-Pollination Gathering: Email 4-5 people from different parts of your life— maybe a coworker, a neighbor, a parent from your kid’s school—and invite them over for wine, tea, or dessert. Let them know the goal: meet someone new, share a story, and just be present. • Creative Shared Moments: Host a craft night, a book swap, a backyard open mic, or even a puzzle-and-popcorn evening. The activity isn’t the point. The point is to gather. • The Five-Minute Favor: Not all connection happens through events. Text someone you haven’t talked to in a while. Offer to run an errand for a busy neighbor. Ask your barista how their week’s been. Micro-acts of community build macro belonging. We’re All Craving It The magic of community isn’t in the epicness—it’s in the shared experience. And now, more than ever, we have to choose to create those experiences. When we do, we tap into something deeply human. Something healing. Something joyful. So what’s your version of a creative community moment? Start small. Stay real. And let it grow. Nina Meehan is a Communication and Creativity Coach and Speaker. https://ninameehan. com/ A block party is a great example of establishing community.
articles.title: Reclaiming community through creative connection

Not the kind you “follow” or “like” online, but the kind where someone borrows a cup of sugar, where kids ride bikes together down the block, where spontaneous laughter rings out over a shared meal. COVID accelerated this disconnection, but even before the pandemic, our shared spaces were already eroding. Busy schedules, digital distractions, and modern life have chipped away at our instinct to gather. But here’s the thing: rebuilding community doesn’t require a huge event or perfectly planned retreat. It just takes intentionality—and a bit of creativity. Creative Simplicity Is the Key We don’t need to add more to our plates—we need to reframe what’s already there. Here are a few easy, creative ways to cultivate real connection: • The Block Party Potluck: Don’t overthink it. Pick a day, put flyers in a few mailboxes or group texts, and ask people to bring a dish. Add chalk for the kids and a Bluetooth speaker for ambiance. Community will take care of the rest. • Cross-Pollination Gathering: Email 4-5 people from different parts of your life— maybe a coworker, a neighbor, a parent from your kid’s school—and invite them over for wine, tea, or dessert. Let them know the goal: meet someone new, share a story, and just be present. • Creative Shared Moments: Host a craft night, a book swap, a backyard open mic, or even a puzzle-and-popcorn evening. The activity isn’t the point. The point is to gather. • The Five-Minute Favor: Not all connection happens through events. Text someone you haven’t talked to in a while. Offer to run an errand for a busy neighbor. Ask your barista how their week’s been. Micro-acts of community build macro belonging. We’re All Craving It The magic of community isn’t in the epicness—it’s in the shared experience. And now, more than ever, we have to choose to create those experiences. When we do, we tap into something deeply human. Something healing. Something joyful. So what’s your version of a creative community moment? Start small. Stay real. And let it grow. articles.text: The Piedmont Recreation Depar tment’s Walking on Wednesdays group announced that it will return to Mountain View Cemetery on April 16 for a special 7th Anniversary Spring Tour, led by author and longtime cemetery docent Dennis Evanosky. This will be Evanosky’s third tour with the group, following well-attended walks in April 2023 and 2024. A historian for the Alameda Post newspaper, Evanosky has “history in his blood” and has written two books about Oakland’s history: Oakland’s Laurel District and Oakland’s Mountain View Cemetery. He has also authored books on Alameda and San Francisco. The April 16 event coincides with the Walking on Wednesdays group’s 7th anniversary. Their first walk took place on April 18, 2018, and a return visit to the cemetery—known for its vibrant spring flowers and expansive views of Oakland, the Bay, and San Francisco—offers a meaningful way to mark the occasion. Instead of meeting at their usual location at the Exedra at Magnolia and Highland Avenues in Piedmont, participants will gather in front of Mountain View Cemetery’s main mausoleum. The tour will begin at 10:30 a.m. and is expected to last about 90 minutes. The cemetery is located at 5000 Piedmont Avenue in Oakland. There is no charge for the event, and free parking is available on the streets inside the cemetery. For more information, contact activity leader Dick Carter at camktgrp@comcast.net. articles.text: Friday, April 4 reawakened perhaps the school’s best rivalry between Piedmont High and Bishop O’Dowd’s boys’ lacrosse teams. The Highlanders defeated the Dragons 8-7 with Timmy Kalamas scoring the game-winner with just 3.6 seconds left, ending a six-game losing streak. In an exhilarating ending, O’Dowd tied the match at 7-7 with 34 seconds left. Sophomore Connor Fredericks won the faceoff, leading to Kalamas scoring in short distance to put the game away. “There were just 20 seconds left and I knew we had one shot. I waited for the clock and took my opportunity. I saw they overcommitted, so I rolled back and went for the goal from there,” Kalamas said of the play. Fredericks claiming the faceoff was a catalyst in the victory. He finished the night 10/18 on draws and lost the preceding faceoff before the final goal. It’s been unusual for Fredericks to lose more than a couple of attempts throughout Piedmont’s nine matches. But taking a line from Apple TV’s Ted Lasso, he kept the memory of a goldfish, and moved on from any frustrating moments. “I knew the pressure was on and that we needed to get down on offense; it led to a great possession by Timmy. I struggled on the face-off whistle a few times, but keeping a goldfish memory really helped to just focus on the next faceoff. Thinking makes you slower,” Fredericks said. It marked the biggest win of first--year coach Paul Pappas’ career, receiving the honorary Gatorade bath after the final buzzer sounded. The PHS Class of 2020 graduate never lost a single match against the Dragons during his playing career, and now his streak remains alive. “Th is why you come back and coach; it was emotional and fun as heck. I’m so proud of them for not giving up and embracing when things got difficult. I’m still undefeated against O’Dowd, just seeing the team happy means Staff Photos Timmy Kalamas (18) runs to midfield after scoring the game-winning goal against Bishop O’Dowd. Connor Fredericks (left) and Timmy Kalamas celebrate a goal against O’Dowd. everything to me,” Pappas said. The victory was a big moment for the Highlanders, showing their most control in possession since former coach Al Yu’s departure in 2023. “We just started doing the little things right and what we’ve been practicing all week. If you win possession and keep possession, you’re going to win a lacrosse game. The attitude switched from playing scared to playing heads-up lacrosse and really pushing for that win,” Pappas said. Senior goalie Gus Von Metzsch was a sophomore on that squad which reached the D2 NCS Championship and won the WACC league championship against O’Dowd. 8-7 over O’Dowd Both teams remained tied 1-1 through the first quarter with a goal from Ian Nguyen, but O’Dowd held PHS scoreless in the second to hold a narrow 2-1 lead at halftime. In the third quarter, the Dragons extended the gap to 3-1 with 9:13 left, but that marked the start of a six-goal scoring run for the Highlanders. From there, Fredericks assisted Nguyen for a goal with 8:21 remaining. After a shot was saved by Von Metzsch, Piedmont scored in transition with 7:02 on the clock. O’Dowd then had a near two-minute possession without a shot, leading to Von Metzsch critically scooping a ground ball near his own goal—turning it into a goal by Brendan Divine with 4:34 left to tie the match at 4-4. Piedmont made quick work of the next possession with Fredericks Head coach Paul Pappas, a PHS Class of 2020, stays undefeated against O’Dowd after finishing his playing career perfect against the Dragons.

articles.text: Miguel Long wins Triple Jump Photos by Becky Spies Miguel Long stands next to his winning mark in the triple jump at the Stanford Invitational. Members of Piedmont’s track and field team traveled to Palo Alto for the Stanford Invitational on Saturday, April 5, competing in eight events throughout the day. The Stanford Invitational brings together some of the best runners throughout the state and is considered among the most prestigious track events on the West Coast. “The Stanford Invitational is such a fun weekend, where elite high school competition from California and neighboring states and we get to warm up and race alongside top tier college athletes. The crowd is engaged, the races lived up to the hype, and everyone keeps their eyes open for runner celebrities. It’s the who’s who of NorCal and beyond. It’s so, so fun to watch,” said PHS coach Pouyan Assadi. It marked a remarkable performance by senior jumper Miguel Long, who won the Triple Jump with a distance of 45 feet, 8.5 inches in a field of 18 athletes. articles.text: Free Community Day is this Sunday, Apr. 13 Ruth Asawa: Retrospective, the first posthumous retrospective of the groundbreaking work of California modernist Ruth Asawa, is now on view at the San Francisco Museum of Modern Art (SFMOMA). Organized by SFMOMA and the Museum of Modern Art in New York, the exhibition features more than 300 works of art, including the looped-wire hanging sculptures for which Asawa is best known. The retrospective also includes drawings, prints, paintings, and archival materials drawn from both public and private collections. “Ruth Asawa: Retrospective is deeply aligned with SFMOMA’s vision to be both local and global—presenting Bay Area artists with profound significance that also have the potential to be highly impactful and relevant on an international scale,” said Christopher Bedford, Helen and Charles Schwab Director of SFMOMA. “This exhibition provides an opportunity to celebrate the legendary Ruth Asawa, who was both a widely acclaimed artist and a hometown inspiration whose impact can be very much felt today.” Spanning more than six decades, the exhibition highlights how Asawa’s longtime San Francisco home and garden served as inspiration for her artistic practice, public sculpture commissions, and tireless advocacy for arts education in the city. The retrospective is co-curated by Janet Bishop, Thomas Weisel Family Chief Curator and Curator of Painting and Sculpture at SFMOMA. “It is an immense privilege to present the full range of Ruth Asawa’s life’s work through this retrospective,” said Bishop. “Not only was Asawa an exceptionally talented artist—among the most distinguished sculptors of the 20th century and a major contributor in so many other mediums—but she lived her values in everything she did, modeling the importance of the arts and opening up creative opportunities for others at every turn.” Ruth Asawa: Retrospective will remain on view through Sept. 2. SFMOMA will offer free admission on Saturday, April 13, to celebrate the exhibition with interactive programming and performances for younger visitors. Admission is also free for residents of the nine Bay Area counties on the first Thursday of each month. Visit sfmoma.org or call 415.357.4000 for more information. articles.text: 1st place: “Beeline to the Blossoms” by Marilyn Wear The California Watercolor Association’s 55th International Exhibition came to a close this past week following a successful and warmly received run at the Piedmont Center for the Arts. The vibrant water-media show featured works by 85 national and international artists, selected by award-winning artist Michael Holter. Of those, 22 pieces received awards chosen by renowned Bay Area artist Gary Bukovnik. During the opening reception, Bukovnik shared insight into the challenge of judging such a high-caliber exhibition. “This exhibition was possibly the most difficult art show for me to judge. There is so much excellence,” he said. When asked about his judging criteria, he added, “Well, aside from my own personal biases—the nature of being human—I like to see that people are able to express their ideas.” The top three awards were presented as follows: • First Place – CWA Gold Award ($2,300): Beeline to the Blossoms by Marilyn Wear • Second Place – CWA Silver Award ($1,800): Orange Blossoms by Chris Krupinski • Third Place – CWA Bronze Award ($1,400): Emigrant Lake Hike by Linda Erfle In addition to juried prizes, attendees of the five-week exhibition were invited to vote for the People’s Choice Award, which was also awarded to second-place winner Chris Krupinski. If you missed the show, you can still see the paintings on CWA’s online gallery at https:// bit.ly/55thShow. If you have any questions or would like more information on a painting, please email sales@californiawatercolor.org. articles.text: Maestro Joseph Young Berkeley Symphony will celebrate the legacy of its fourth Music Director, Maestro Joseph Young, at its 2025 Spring Gala on Saturday, May 10, at the Unitarian Universalist Church in Kensington. Young first guest-conducted the symphony in 2019 as an emergency substitute and was soon invited to become its next music director—his first appointment in that role—following the success of that initial concert. In November 2024, the symphony announced that Young will conclude his tenure at the end of the current season. During his leadership, Young guided the orchestra through the challenges of the COVID-19 pandemic and widespread performing arts venue closures. He launched digital programming initiatives and secured key grants to promote diversity and equity within the orchestra’s staff and musician ranks. In the 2024–25 season, Young has continued to grow his national and international profile with debuts and return engagements at the National Philharmonic, Orquesta Sinfónica RTVE, the Royal Liverpool Philharmonic, and the Louisville Orchestra, among others. The 2025 gala will be hosted by Dianne Nicolini, midday host on KDFC Classical California, and will include live performances by Berkeley Symphony musicians and special guest artists. The evening will feature a hilltop reception with sweeping views of the Bay Area, along with hors d’oeuvres, an open bar, and a three-course dinner catered by Carrie Dove Catering. Guests can sponsor a table or purchase individual tickets, starting at $500. To learn more or make a sponsorship gift, email Gillian Eorwyn, Director of Development and Communications, at georwyn@berkeleysymphony.org or call 510-841- 2800.

articles.text: San Francisco Ballet is honoring the legacy of esteemed Dutch choreographer Hans van Manen with a mixed-bill program titled Van Manen: Dutch Grandmaster, on stage now through April 19 at the War Memorial Opera House. The program features a selection of van Manen’s most acclaimed ballets, including Grosse Fuge, Variations for Two Couples, Solo, and, making its San Francisco premiere, 5 Tangos. Curated by San Francisco Ballet Artistic Director Tamara Rojo, the program showcases a blend of classical and contemporary styles, set to music by composers such as Astor Piazzolla, Bach, and Beethoven. “Hans van Manen is the most important choreographer of the Dutch tradition, and we are thrilled to bring four works from his oeuvre to San Francisco,” Rojo said. “His legacy is unparalleled, shaping what we think of now as the signature Dutch style. What appears to be simple choreography is actually quite difficult to perform.” Rojo added that the works “[focus] on musicality and powerful exchanges of energy between humans, [and] allow the ComPhoto by Lindsey Rallo Dores André and Esteban Hernández in van Manen’s 5 Tango’s pany to showcase their charisma, top-tier virtuosity, and individuality.” “It’s a wonderful opportunity to witness SF Ballet’s dancers take on a uniquely European style,” she said. Dores André, Max Cauthorn, Sasha De Sola, Nikisha Fogo, Jasmine Jimison, Wona Park, Jennifer Stahl, Joseph Walsh, and Wei Wang make their role debuts as Principal dancers in ‘Van Manen: Dutch Grandmaster.’ Performance showtimes vary. articles.text: Registration for free event is recommended San Francisco Opera’s highly anticipated Bohéme Out of the Box returns to Sausalito in Marin County on Saturday, April 26, and Sunday, April 27. The company’s acclaimed musicians and singers will perform an abridged version of Giacomo Puccini’s La Bohème just steps from downtown Sausalito’s picturesque waterfront, with sweeping views of San Francisco Bay as a backdrop. This 70-minute traveling production is performed live on a mobile stage crafted from a repurposed shipping container and features musical excerpts from La Bohème sung in Italian. English narration will be available through guests’ cell phones. Originally conceived as part of San Francisco Opera’s 100th anniversary season, Bohéme Out of the Box continues to engage audiences across the Bay Area, with recent performances in Hayward and San Ramon. Sausalito guests are encouraged to pack a picnic or enjoy food and beverages from the many nearby restaurants along Bridgeway. Chairs will be available on a first-come, first-served basis at the parking lot performance site, but attendees are welcome to bring their own seating. Both performances begin at 2 p.m. and will take place in the parking lot adjacent to the Sausalito Center for the Arts. Guests are also invited to visit the gallery space, which will be showcasing work from more than 250 artists participating in Marin Open Studios. Bohéme Out of the Box is presented in partnership with the Sausalito Paks and Recreation Department and the Sausalito Center for the Arts. Families with young children are invited to participate in free “First Act Workshops” 30 minutes prior to each performance. Bohème Out of the Box is a free event. Registration at sfopera.com/box is now available and encouraged but not required. San Francisco Opera’s free production is performed on a mobile stage made from a repurposed shipping container.

articles.text: The Fort Mason Center for Arts & Culture (FMCAC) in San Francisco is launching a new series of monthly nighttime events beginning Friday, April 18, in partnership with Off the Grid and West Coast Craft. Fort Mason Night Market 2025 was developed following the success of an inaugural December night market that drew more than 10,000 attendees. Beginning April 18 and continuing monthly through December, FMCAC will host outdoor markets that transform its iconic waterfront campus into a lively showcase of local artisans, cuisine, and live entertainment. “Fort Mason Center is known for being a gathering place—a space for people to exchange ideas, experience beauty, and connect with different modes of art and cultural expressions,” said Mike Buhler, FMCAC’s president and CEO. “We’re excited to collaborate with our partners to offer another way for people to come together, support local arts organizations and small businesses, and enjoy the natural beauty of the campus.” Off the Grid will feature more than 25 food and refreshment vendors at each event, while attendees can enjoy performances by local DJs, participate in hands-on creative workshops, and view public art installations from FMCAC’s collections. West Coast Craft—founded in San Francisco in 2013 to provide a platform for independent artists and designers—will also take part. Known for one of the largest arts fairs in the country, West Coast Craft traditionally hosts its annual summer event at FMCAC. Artisans who appear at that festival will be invited to showcase and sell their work at the monthly Night Market. “This new market is an exciting evolution of what we started back in 2010 with the original Off the Grid festival [in San Francisco],” said Matt Cohen, founder of Off the Grid. “This time around, we’re expanding our offerings to include both crowd favorites and emerging food creators, plus joining forces with West Coast Craft and FMCAC to offer an interactive shopping, dining, artistic, and community experience—a perfect blend that is quintessentially San Francisco.” Paulina Nassar, co-founder of West Coast Craft, said the collaboration creates “an incredible opportunity for our community of artists and designers to connect with their customers in a new, vibrant format—shopping from exceptional vendors while enjoying the arts programming and amazing dining options that make Fort Mason a unique destination.” All events begin at 4 p.m., are free and open to the public. Night Markets are held on the following dates: April 18, May 30, June 27, July 18, August (Date TBA), September 5, October 17, November (Date TBA), and December 12, 2025. For more information, visit https://fortmason.org/event/fortmason-night-market-2025/. Fort Mason’s inaugural night market in December 2024 drew over 10,000 attendees.

The image of a raptor’s unblinking eye or a torso dangling from its jaws still lingers in pop culture memory. At its core, the Jurassic series, like Jaws before it, taps into a timeless fear: a predator unleashed, and humans rendered helpless in the face of nature’s ancient power. That sense of overwhelming vulnerability is the franchise’s enduring magic. And while every installment since has varied in tone and scale, together they’ve built a surprisingly durable—and consistently thrilling— cinematic universe. The latest chapter, Jurassic World: Fallen Kingdom, is the second film in the new trilogy that began with Jurassic World. Absent the fantastical, devoid of that floating sense of the surreal so often embedded in Studio Ghibli’s animated features, Poppy Hill is a touching, straight-forward, unsentimental coming-of-age story about a strong-willed 16-year-old girl named Umi (Sarah Bolger) who meets and become much enamored with Shun (Anton Melchin), a member of a geeky group of boys who inhabit an aging wreck of a building out of which they run a newspaper of which he is the editor. The story is set in Yokohama, over looking a sweeping bay. The year is 1963, and Japan is only just beginning to fully emerge from the devastation wrought by WWII. Umi, whose father was lost at sea, and her mother is presently studying in America, helps her grandmother (Jamie Lee Curtis) run a boarding house. She is responsible for much of the cleaning and shopping while attending a nearby high school and struggling to keep up with her schoolwork. In the opening scenes, we see Umi raising a flag in homage to her much missed father. She is spotted by Shun who works on his father’s tugboat. A scene from Miyazaki’s From Up on Poppy Hill Umi soon meets Shun and learns about his and his friends’ resistance to the razing of an old building they occupy as part of urban renewal. The struggle is between reverence for the past and the urge by officials to move toward a new, more modern Japan. The Olympics is slated to arrive in Japan in 1964. Umi joins Shun and friends in a campaign protesting the removal of the building and the more time she and Shun spend together the deeper their connection grows, and soon the story finds that tentative teenage romance sweet spot. However, not atypical for Studio Ghibli, screenwriter Hayao Miyazaki introduces a plot curve that causes Umi and Shun deep consternation, information that they find all but impossible to resolve. Of course, the hand-drawn animation of Up on Poppy Hill is as good as any work produced by the Studio, the characters are appealing, the background images wonderfully created. Also not surprising, is that the story stresses the power of goodness while being, in its special way, light and breezy and filled with youthful idealism leavened by a certain wistfulness. The public lost its taste for balloon ascensions in Blair Park after little Bertram’s death, and the ascensions in Blair Park ended shortly thereafter. What Became of Blair Park? As fine as the intentions of the park operators were, Blair Park seems to have encountered problems almost immediately. In 1892, the Oakland Tribune reported that “gamblers had things their own way up at Blair Park” and described prospering shell games. Citizens were also concerned that the planned casino would attract “scum and hoodlum.” In 1896 the Board of Directors of Mountain View Cemetery complained that “the balloon ascensions on Sundays from Blair Park is [sic] becoming a great nuisance, attracting a great crowd of the hoodlum element and causing a disturbance in the Cemetery Grounds.” They called on the Sheriff to protect the cemetery grounds and arrest trespassers. The fate of Blair Park was tied to the fiscal success of the Consolidated Piedmont Cable Company. In 1892, electric trolleys were replacing the cable cars and competing for ridership. Due to the great expense of building the cable line, the Piedmont Cable Company went into receivership in 1893, and the assets were sold at auction in 1895. Walter Blair’s heirs continued to own the park land, but it was heavily mortgaged. In 1897 all of Blair’s 235 acres, including Blair Park, were for sale. articles.text: Photo by Deborah Quok Smoked Salmon and Asparagus Mini-Frittatas Springtime means brunch time for many of us. And finally, we are slated for some dry and sunny days to gather with family and friends. I often make a frittata for our Sunday brunch. It’s usually in a 12-inch skillet to savor leftovers the next day. I’ve modified a springtime favorite to bake in muffin tins for individual servings, ideal for entertaining and your brunch spread. Advance notes: It’s important to liberally grease each muffin cup, even if for “nonstick” pans. If well buttered or oiled, the muffins are removed easily. Omit this if using parchment liners. I add the salmon, asparagus pieces (saving the tips for topping), crumbled cheese and chives into the egg mixture; just as I do for a large frittata. For mini-frittatas, carefully fill each cup with about the same amounts of everything in each. If you want to be more precise, layer the fillings before adding the egg mix as follows: asparagus pieces, salmon pieces, crumbled cheese and lastly chives on top. Smoked Salmon and Asparagus Mini-Frittatas Serves 12 INGREDIENTS • 10 large eggs • 1/2 cup whole milk • 4 ounces cold smoked, sliced sockeye salmon • 12 stalks asparagus, about the diameter of a pencil. • 2.5 ounces goat cheese, crumbled (about 1/3 cup) • 1/4 cup fresh chives, cut into 1/4-inch lengths • 1/2 teaspoon black pepper, freshly ground • 1/4 teaspoon sea salt, or to taste • 2 teaspoons olive oil, extra-virgin • Vegetable oil spray or butter for greasing the muffin tins. Omit if using parchment liners. INSTRUCTIONS Prepare a 12-cup muffin pan by liberally greasing each cup or use parchment liners. Position an oven rack to the lower third position. Preheat the oven to 425°F. Cut a 1-1/2 inch length of the asparagus tips off, then cut the remaining stalks into 1/2-inch pieces to measure a generous one-half cup of pieces. Heat the 2 teaspoons of olive oil in a small skillet over medium heat. Add all the asparagus pieces and sauté until just tender. Remove from heat and set aside. Separate the asparagus tips from the 1/2-inch pieces, the tips will be used to decorate the tops of each frittata. Cut the smoked salmon into 1/2-inch squares by first cutting the entire piece of adhered sliced salmon in half lengthwise. Stack the two pieces atop each other, then cut in 1/2-inch strips lengthwise. Turn the strips 90-degrees and cut these strips crosswise in 1/2-inch increments. Gently separate the slices. It’s OK if there are a few of the thin slices stick together. Whisk together the eggs, milk, salt, and pepper in a large bowl. Add the salmon, asparagus pieces, cheese, and chives and stir to evenly distribute. (Optional: see the advance note above to layer the filling.) Divide evenly among muffin cups, leaving about 1/4-inch from the rim. Bake for 10 minutes, then remove the muffin pan to place an asparagus tip atop each mini frittata. Return to the oven, continue baking until the frittatas are lightly browned, set in the center, and puffed up. Total baking time is about 18 – 20 minutes. (Their puffy splendor is temporary, as they will fall to about even to the rim upon removal from the oven.) Transfer the muffin pan to a wire rack and cool for 10 minutes. Use a small silicone spatula to loosen around the edges and bottoms of each tin. Remove gently and serve warm. Previously printed in the Piedmont Post on April 5, 2023.

articles.text: The first Wednesday of April seemed to be time for the Walking on Wednesdays group to do its annual spring check of the Piedmont real estate market. Everyone seems to enjoy seeing homes that are for sale, and there was a good turnout of 38 walkers and three K-9 best friends at the Exedra. Before the group started some information on the national and local real estate market was provided. A study from Bankrate, a financial services company, reported the median price of a U.S. home listed for sale was $418,000. But an article last week in the San Francisco Chronicle said that according to Zillow data the typical high-tier home in the San Francisco metropolitan area in February 2025 was worth $1.91 million. That’s almost 4% higher than in February 2024. Low-tier home values essentially stayed flat at just over $700,000. High mortgage rates are a main driver for this. Rates are twice what they were five years ago, and they’ve kept first-time home buyers and homeowners unwilling to give up their lower mortgage rates out of the market. Wealthier buyers have the resources to make all-cash offers, or large down payments that reduce their monthly costs. Twenty-six percent of homes sold in 2024 were all cash offers. The luxury home inventory is also especially tight, even by Bay Area standards, making this part of the market more competitive. The other major factor is the stock market. Buyers with large sums in stocks, including tech employees with stock options, have benefited from the market’s performance over the last two years, and are able to purchase expensive homes. For Piedmont, Calia Homes did some research and found that based on Multiple Listing Service (MLS) data for the 20 years from 2005 to 2024, the median sales price of Piedmont homes grew 73% from $1,420,000 to $2,450,000.
